catalog_quote: 1.0. A description of Kinga must have a stage at which every word will have one and only one syllable segment that bears a high tone. This high tone may occur in one out of three possible positions: (i) on the ante-penultimate (APU), or (ii) on the pre-stem initial (PSI), or (iii) on the penultimate (PU) syllabic segment. These positions must be counted in moras, not in syllables. Long vowels will be regarded as two vowels (cf. 2.1). ... Kinga obviously has a surface constraint that does not permit high tone on a word final syllable. ... 2.2. ... The assignment of high tone to the next to last mora of a word (pattern PU) has been shown as of rather restricted occurrence. Besides in a marginal (and doubtful?) group of nouns we find it regularly in a group of negative tenses. ... 2.3. The reduced tone system of Kinga. sweep_summary: Kinga (nucl1379) is in the catalog as tonal (restricted/culminative H) on Schadeberg 1973. this search of works with stress in the title had one title item, Philippson's 1991 Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East African Bantu; an open author's PDF exists at ddl.cnrs.fr (HEAD 200 today), was already held by the project from a parallel search, and was copied into the nucl1379 folder and read. Kinga is treated at pp. 272-274 (Ch. 4 sec. 6.2.2.2), pp. 444-446 (Ch. 6 sec. 2.6.2) and p. 508 (Annexe): one H per word, on the antepenultimate mora by default, on the pre-stem mora in some tenses and on the stem penult in negative tenses, long vowels counting two moras; Philippson labels the system 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H' and lists Kinga among languages for which he used his own field notes (p. 515). This refines the catalog (adds an accentual/metrical label and independent partly first-hand confirmation of the three placement patterns) without contradicting it; Schadeberg 1973 remains the deciding source. Files already held by the project from our reading of 9/16 (Hyman 2006, Hyman 2017, Wolff 1905) were re-checked: Hyman 2006 discusses Kinga as an obligatory-H mora-counting restricted tone system (pp. 228, 240-242, 245), Hyman 2017 does not mention Kinga, Wolff 1905 marks no tone and only notes that the penult is regularly long (Lautlehre sec. 1). written at Nothing remains unread; works still to obtain (Schadeberg 1971 dissertation, Odden 1988, Kaehler-Meyer 1969) were not in this search of works with stress in the title's title list and stay print only at low priority.

new_statements.quote: « Si nous prenons le cas du kinga (groupe XV), nous constatons d'abord que tous les verbo-nominaux de la langue présentent le même schème accentuel, à savoir accent sur la more anté-pénultième [...] Toutes les voyelles longues (y compris celles longues par position devant mi-nasale) comptent pour deux mores [...] Cependant, un certain nombre d'autres tiroirs sont accentués sur la more précédant immédiatement le thème minimal [...] Une autre catégorie de tiroirs (il s'agit d'ailleurs uniquement de négatifs) sont toujours accentués sur la pénultième du thème [...] Quoi qu'il en soit, les mots en kinga ne peuvent jamais porter plus d'un H »
new_statements.translation: If we take the case of Kinga (group XV), we first note that all the verbo-nominals [infinitives] of the language show the same accentual pattern, namely accent on the antepenultimate mora [...] All long vowels (including those long by position before a prenasalised consonant) count as two moras [...] However, a number of other tenses are accented on the mora immediately preceding the minimal stem [...] Another category of tenses (in fact only negatives) are always accented on the penult of the stem [...] In any case, words in Kinga can never carry more than one H.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V; theses.fr 1992PA05H011. Author's PDF, http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/Fulltext/philippson/these.pdf
new_statements.locator: Ch. 4 sec. 6.2.2.2, pp. 272-274 (with Annexe p. 508 and Ch. 6 sec. 2.6.2 p. 444)
new_statements.reading: A partly first-hand (author's own field notes, p. 515) statement that Kinga has a single culminative H per word placed by mora count: antepenultimate mora by default, pre-stem mora in certain tenses, stem-penultimate mora in negative tenses. Philippson calls this an H-melody accent system ('langue accentuelle à mélodie H', p. 508) rather than a restricted tone system, but the placement facts are exactly Schadeberg's APU/PSI/PU patterns, so the statement confirms the catalog's tonal-or-pitch accent coding and refines its typological label; it gives no evidence of stress or of penultimate metrics (p. 488: penultimate metric 'possible, mais sans vraie confirmation' for Kinga).

audit.reasoning: The record rests on Schadeberg 1973 (SAL 4.1), the dedicated, fieldwork-based and universally cited description of Kinga word prosody; we hold the open PDF and the deciding quotation is verbatim at sect. 1.0 p. 24, tense (12) p. 33, sect. 2.2 p. 37 and 2.3 p. 38 (locator says pp. 38-41; 2.2 actually begins p. 37, trivial). Coding 'tonal' (culminative/obligatory one-H-per-word, mora-counted APU default, PSI marked, PU restricted) with qv tonal-OR-pitch accent matches the source and is independently endorsed by Hyman 2006 (downloaded now), who calls Kinga analytically indeterminate between restricted tone/PA/SA but concludes it is tonal and 'cannot be SA' because H is assigned by mora (pp. 228, 230, 242, 245). sources.note: Kinga has no stress accent; it has one culminative H per word whose position is counted in moras: default on the antepenultimate mora (all infinitives, most tenses), on the mora immediately before the minimal stem in some tenses (future, hypothetical), and on the stem penult in a set of negative tenses. sources.quote: No tone marking and no word-accent rule (confirms Schadeberg's remark that Wolff describes Kinga 'without reference to tone'). Only: 'die vorletzte Silbe eines jeden Wortes [ist] der Regel nach lang' (penult regularly long, sect. 1) and '-vuli bleibt stets unbetont, und der Wortton rueckt auf das vorhergehende Wort, und zwar zumeist auf die letzte Silbe'.
